praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: During a Part C home visit, a 14-month-old watches the specialist hide a rattle under a blanket, then pulls the blanket off and grabs it. What does this most clearly indicate about development?

options.a: Object permanence is emerging as the child learns through sensory-motor action
options.b: Conservation of volume and number is already stable, as in concrete operations
options.c: Symbolic pretend play and egocentric speech now dominate thinking
options.d: Hypothetical-deductive reasoning about unseen possibilities is available

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Searching for a hidden object is a classic sensorimotor (birth–~2) milestone: the toddler is constructing object permanence through action on the environment. Conservation belongs to concrete operations, pretend/egocentrism to preoperational thought, and hypothetico-deductive reasoning to formal operations.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses sensorimotor action with concrete operations; conservation of quantity appears around ages 7–11, not at 14 months.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses this age with the preoperational stage (about 2–7), when symbolic play and egocentrism are typical.
distractorExplanations.d: Assigns formal-operational hypothetical reasoning (about age 11+) to an infant still in the sensorimotor period.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A 4th grader with autism follows a picture schedule in general education but sobs when a substitute skips morning meeting without warning. Which response best supports this student in an inclusive class?

options.a: Insert extra unannounced schedule changes so the student practices flexibility by exposure
options.b: Preview the change with the visual schedule and a short social script before class
options.c: Remove the picture schedule this week so the student relies only on spoken directions
options.d: Place the student in a large unsupervised group activity to force social exposure

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Visual schedules, priming, and explicit social scripts are evidence-based supports that let many students with autism stay in general education when routines shift. Surprise changes, early fading of visuals, and unsupported group exposure typically raise anxiety rather than teach flexibility.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats surprise as the teaching method; flexibility is built by priming and gradual change, not unannounced disruption.
distractorExplanations.c: Visual supports are an evidence-based practice; stripping them to force verbal-only following undermines access.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses inclusion with unsupported exposure; social skills need explicit instruction, not a sink-or-swim group.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A 4-year-old is substantially below age expectations in walking, combining words, and feeding with a spoon. The preschool team is weighing IDEA eligibility. Which statement is most accurate?

options.a: Identify specific learning disability because later reading and math are likely at risk
options.b: Classify intellectual disability from a single IQ near 70, without reviewing domains
options.c: Consider developmental delay when one or more developmental domains are substantially delayed
options.d: Wait until after age 9, then evaluate adaptive behavior as the only domain of concern

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: IDEA’s developmental delay category (available through age 9, used mainly in early childhood) is based on substantial delay in one or more domains: physical, cognitive, communication, social-emotional, or adaptive. Academic SLD, IQ-only ID, and an after-age-9 adaptive-only wait misstate both the construct and the age window.

distractorExplanations.a: SLD is an unexpected academic deficit after instruction; motor, language, and self-care delays are developmental domains, not SLD.
distractorExplanations.b: Intellectual disability requires significantly subaverage intellectual functioning plus adaptive deficits, not an IQ number alone.
distractorExplanations.d: The delay category is used through age 9 across domains; adaptive behavior is only one domain, not a post-age-9 exclusive gate.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: During partner reading, a 2nd grader with autism keeps offering the page the student prefers, even after the partner said, “I want the dinosaur book.” What skill is most clearly impaired?

options.a: Decoding of print despite typically developing insight into what peers want
options.b: Holding multi-step directions in working memory while finishing a worksheet
options.c: Planning and coordinating gross-motor sequences on playground equipment
options.d: Understanding another person’s perspective, beliefs, and desires (theory of mind)

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Theory of mind is the ability to represent others’ beliefs and wants as different from one’s own. Persistently offering the preferred page after an explicit contrary request is a perspective-taking failure, not a decoding, working-memory, or motor-planning problem.

distractorExplanations.a: Decoding with intact social insight describes a reading disability profile, not difficulty tracking another child’s stated desire.
distractorExplanations.b: Working memory holds steps of a task; here the peer’s desire was stated once and still not used.
distractorExplanations.c: Gross-motor planning (dyspraxia/DCD) does not explain failing to use a partner’s spoken preference.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A 17-year-old with intellectual disability is in a high school program that still includes functional academics. Which instructional emphasis is still required under IDEA?

options.a: Transition planning for post-school living, employment, and community participation
options.b: Academic content only, because functional skills instruction ends after elementary school
options.c: Preschool self-help drills repeated until mental age equals chronological age
options.d: Vocational training withheld until the student exits public school at age 22

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: IDEA requires transition services in the IEP no later than age 16 (earlier in many states). Adolescents with intellectual disability still need age-appropriate instruction in living, work, and community participation; functional skills do not expire in elementary school, and vocational prep is not postponed until exit.

distractorExplanations.b: Functional and community skills continue through secondary school; they are not an elementary-only curriculum.
distractorExplanations.c: Best practice is chronological-age-appropriate, functional content—not repeating preschool tasks to match mental age.
distractorExplanations.d: Transition and vocational instruction occur during school; waiting until age-22 exit violates the IEP timeline.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: Parents of a 22-month-old with documented motor and communication delays ask which system should evaluate the child first. What is the correct answer?

options.a: IDEA Part B preschool special education run by the public elementary school
options.b: IDEA Part C early intervention for infants and toddlers with delays or disabilities
options.c: A school-age IEP under Part B serving students from age 6 through 21
options.d: Adult vocational rehabilitation authorized under the Rehabilitation Act

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: IDEA Part C covers early intervention for infants and toddlers (birth to age 3) with disabilities or developmental delays, typically through an IFSP. Part B §619 is preschool ages 3–5, school-age IEPs are Part B 6–21, and adult VR is not an IDEA infant program.

distractorExplanations.a: Preschool special education (Part B, Section 619) starts at age 3; this child is still in the Part C age range.
distractorExplanations.c: School-age IEP services under Part B begin after early childhood; Part C ends at the third birthday.
distractorExplanations.d: Vocational rehabilitation serves eligible adults/youth under the Rehabilitation Act, not infants under Part C.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A 5th grader with ADHD starts a three-part science lab, then blurts to a neighbor and cannot return to the next step after a redirect. Which skill set is most involved?

options.a: Phonological awareness, decoding accuracy, and oral reading fluency
options.b: Fine-motor control, visual tracking, and handwriting speed on the data sheet
options.c: Working memory for steps, inhibiting blurts, and shifting back to the lab
options.d: Crystallized knowledge: stored science facts and general information

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Holding the next step, stopping an off-task blurt, and switching back after a redirect are core executive functions: working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility. Literacy subprocesses, visual-motor skills, and stored knowledge are different constructs.

distractorExplanations.a: These are early reading skills; the breakdown is self-regulation of a multi-step lab, not decoding.
distractorExplanations.b: OT-related motor and visual-motor skills do not explain blurting and failing to shift back to the procedure.
distractorExplanations.d: Crystallized knowledge is accumulated information on IQ-type tasks, not the control processes that sequence behavior.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: After a tumble in the block area, a toddler glances at the familiar teacher, accepts a brief hug, then returns to building. Attachment theory best explains this as:

options.a: Evidence that responsive care mainly accelerates cognition rather than emotional bonds
options.b: Proof that consistent caregiving creates dependence and delays independent exploration
options.c: A pattern that becomes educationally relevant only after the child enters formal school
options.d: Secure attachment, with the adult serving as a safe base for continued exploration

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Bowlby and Ainsworth describe secure attachment as using a consistent caregiver as a safe base: the child seeks comfort, then resumes exploration. Responsive care builds that bond in infancy; it does not primarily “raise IQ,” create clingy dependence, or wait until kindergarten to matter.

distractorExplanations.a: Attachment theory’s core claim is about emotional bonds and felt security, not cognition as the main outcome.
distractorExplanations.b: Secure attachment typically increases exploration from a safe base; it does not lock the child into dependence.
distractorExplanations.c: Attachment organizes in infancy and early childhood; waiting until school entry misses the sensitive caregiving window.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A 4th grader leaves the seat during independent work, blurts answers, and misses multi-step directions, but decodes on grade level and chats reciprocally with peers. Which profile fits best?

options.a: ADHD: inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that impair school functioning
options.b: Autism: social-communication deficits plus restricted, repetitive interests
options.c: Specific learning disability in reading after adequate instruction still fails decoding
options.d: Bipolar disorder: discrete manic elevation alternating with periods of depression

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: The pattern is inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that interfere with classwork, with intact decoding and reciprocal social chat. That matches ADHD (often served under OHI), not autism’s social-communication/restricted-interest criteria, SLD-reading, or episodic mania/depression.

distractorExplanations.b: Autism requires persistent social-communication deficits and restricted interests; reciprocal peer chat argues against that.
distractorExplanations.c: Grade-level decoding rules out the classic unexpected reading-decoding SLD profile.
distractorExplanations.d: Bipolar disorder is episodic mood elevation and depression, not a daily seat-leaving and blurting pattern.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: At a 12-month Part C review, the child says “dada,” turns when named, and hands a ball when asked. Which milestone statement is most accurate?

options.a: Two-word combinations such as “more milk” are already expected by 12 months
options.b: First words plus understanding of simple requests are typical around 12 months
options.c: A 50-word vocabulary with two-word sentences is the 12-month language standard
options.d: Cooing without a consistent response to name is still typical at 12 months

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Around 12 months many children use a few true words and follow simple requests while responding to name. Two-word phrases and a ~50-word vocabulary are closer to 18–24 months; absent name response by 12 months is a red flag, not typical.

distractorExplanations.a: Two-word combinations typically emerge around 18–24 months, not by the first birthday.
distractorExplanations.c: A 50-word lexicon with word combinations is a roughly 24-month milestone, not a 12-month standard.
distractorExplanations.d: Name response usually appears by 6–9 months; missing it at 12 months warrants follow-up, not reassurance.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A 2nd grader in an inclusive class covers ears in the cafeteria, chews shirt cuffs, and refuses glue and clothing tags. How should the team interpret this pattern?

options.a: The student shows no reaction to sound, touch, or visual input in any setting
options.b: The pattern can influence only math computation, not other classroom routines
options.c: The student is seeking or avoiding particular sounds, textures, or lights
options.d: Sensory differences by themselves cancel any remaining need for IEP services

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Covering ears (auditory avoidance), chewing cuffs (oral seeking), and refusing glue/tags (tactile avoidance) are sensory modulation differences. They can affect cafeteria, art, and clothing—not “no sensation,” not math-only, and they do not erase eligibility or supports.

distractorExplanations.a: Hyporesponsiveness to all input is not this picture; the student is reacting strongly to specific stimuli.
distractorExplanations.b: Sensory differences show up in lunch, materials, and clothing, not as a math-computation-only issue.
distractorExplanations.d: Sensory needs may be addressed on an IEP or 504; they do not automatically end special education services.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A student with a learning disability cannot complete a two-step word problem independently but succeeds after the teacher models a graphic organizer and then fades prompts. Where is this instruction placed?

options.a: Outside the zone: the task remains impossible even with expert modeling and prompts
options.b: Below the zone: the student already completes the same task fully independently
options.c: Piaget-matched: the task was chosen only because it fits a labeled cognitive stage
options.d: Inside Vygotsky’s ZPD: possible with guidance, not yet independent

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: The zone of proximal development is the gap between unaided performance and performance with scaffolding. Success with a modeled organizer that is then faded is instruction inside the ZPD. Tasks already mastered or still impossible even with help sit outside that zone; Piagetian stage-matching is a different theory.

distractorExplanations.a: If expert help still fails, the task is beyond the ZPD; here the student succeeds with modeling.
distractorExplanations.b: Independent mastery is below the ZPD; this student still needs the organizer to succeed.
distractorExplanations.c: Matching work to a Piagetian stage is not Vygotsky’s ZPD, which is defined by assisted versus independent performance.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A kindergartner with hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, and a documented extra copy of chromosome 21 receives special education. What is the etiology?

options.a: Trisomy 21, the chromosomal pattern associated with Down syndrome
options.b: A 45,X karyotype associated with Turner syndrome in phenotypic females
options.c: A CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 associated with fragile X syndrome
options.d: A paternal 15q11-q13 deletion associated with Prader-Willi syndrome

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Down syndrome is caused by an extra chromosome 21 (trisomy 21 in most cases; translocation and mosaicism are less common). The listed alternatives are distinct genetic conditions with different chromosomal mechanisms and classroom profiles.

distractorExplanations.b: 45,X (missing one X) is Turner syndrome, not Down syndrome.
distractorExplanations.c: A CGG expansion in FMR1 causes fragile X, a common inherited cause of intellectual disability, not trisomy 21.
distractorExplanations.d: A paternal 15q11-q13 deletion causes Prader-Willi syndrome, not Down syndrome.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A kindergartner on a speech-language IEP cannot blend onset-rime or map letters to sounds, though oral vocabulary is growing. Which skills should the special educator treat as reading prerequisites?

options.a: Fluent cursive handwriting plus accurate spelling of weekly grade-level lists
options.b: Phonological awareness, letter-sound knowledge, and continuing vocabulary growth
options.c: Memorizing whole-word lists before any instruction in letter-sound correspondences
options.d: Silent-reading stamina and grade-level comprehension strategy instruction

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Foundational reading depends on phonological awareness, the alphabetic principle (letter-sound knowledge), and oral language/vocabulary. Handwriting and spelling develop alongside or after early reading; whole-word-first instruction and silent-stamina/comprehension strategies are not prerequisites for beginning decoding.

distractorExplanations.a: Cursive and spelling lists are not prerequisites for learning to decode; they typically develop with or after early reading.
distractorExplanations.c: Science of reading rejects whole-word memorization as the first step before letter-sound instruction.
distractorExplanations.d: Stamina and comprehension strategies are later reading outcomes, not the skills this kindergartner still lacks.

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.prompt: A 3rd grader with a mild intellectual disability is progressing in general education with a paraeducator and modified assignments. A parent requests a self-contained class “so specialists can work without interruptions.” What does LRE require?

options.a: Change to the self-contained class now because a restrictive setting is automatically better
options.b: Permit general education only when the student needs no supplementary aids or services
options.c: Keep general education with supports unless data show a more restrictive setting is required
options.d: Treat LRE as mandatory full-time inclusion for every student without individual analysis

praxis-special-education-readiness-check.explanation: Least restrictive environment means educating the student with nondisabled peers to the maximum extent appropriate, with supplementary aids and services. Inclusion with a paraeducator and modifications is LRE when the student is making progress. LRE is not “more separate is better,” not “gen-ed only if no supports,” and not automatic 100% inclusion for every child.

distractorExplanations.a: A more restrictive placement is justified only if FAPE cannot be provided with supports in a less restrictive setting.
distractorExplanations.b: Supplementary aids (paraeducator, modifications) are how LRE is implemented; needing them does not bar general education.
distractorExplanations.d: LRE is individualized; full-time inclusion is not mandated when a student needs a different mix of settings for FAPE.
